sentences.text: The Cuban giant owl was an extinct genus of owls that stood 1.1 meters tall, a height estimated by Arredondo.
While initially estimated at 30 kg, later studies suggest the animal's body mass was between 9 and 13.5 kg, though it is believed the owl likely weighed over 9 kg.
This species featured very large and powerfully built legs and feet, with females being larger than males.
Evidence suggests the animal may have been capable of killing prey weighing 35 kg or more.
Remains are found abundantly across the island, with at least three nearly complete skeletons discovered.
When the first specimen was described in the 1950s, its large bones led to it being classified as a member of the family Phorusrhacidae.
In 1961, Pierce Brodkorb correctly identified the fossils as belonging to an owl.
A 2020 study concluded that previously described species were synonyms of O. oteroi and described a new valid species, O. ewingi, from material once assigned to Bubo osvaldoi.
The animal had a reduced keel on its sternum, suggesting it may have been capable of short bursts of flight.
It is probable that the animal only flew when extremely pressed, preferring to run like a modern wild turkey.
It was probably an ambush predator that pounced on unsuspecting prey with its crushing talons.
It is believed the animal primarily preyed on large rodents like Heteropsomys and Macrocapromys, as well as medium-sized mammals such as ground sloths.
The animal belongs to the class Aves, order Strigiformes, and family Strigidae.
The type species is O. oteroi, described by Arredondo in 1954, while O. minor, O. gigas, and O. acevedoi were described by Arredondo in 1982.
Remains of the animal have been found in cave deposits dating from 126,000 to 11,700 years ago on the island of Cuba.
The time range of the genus spans from the Gelasian to the Holocene, approximately 2.58 to 0 million years ago.
